data.title: Project data
data.what: The respondent-level data file this project holds: one row per respondent, one column per answer.
data.why: Every check, table, cleaning step and report reads this one file, so they always agree.
data.how: Upload the export from Decipher, Qualtrics or SPSS (.xlsx, .sav, .csv). Replacing it re-runs everything on the new file.

notice.title: Consent and notice
notice.what: Checks what respondents are told before they agree, against India’s DPDP Act (and, for health studies, the side-effect reporting statement).
notice.why: Collecting personal data without a proper notice and consent is unlawful, and a client audit will ask for it.
notice.how: Items marked ○ are missing. Fill in your organisation, purpose and contact, then “Add notice and consent question” puts both screens first.

quote.title: Quote from the questionnaire
quote.what: An estimate of interview length from the questionnaire itself, the screeners that decide who qualifies, and — from your rates — the sample cost.
quote.why: Bids are usually priced on a guessed length; a study bid at 12 minutes that runs 17 is under-priced for every complete.
quote.how: Enter completes and incidence to see how many people must start; add your rate per minute to see cost per complete and total.

incidence.title: Incidence
incidence.what: The share of people who start the survey and qualify (are not screened out).
incidence.why: Low incidence means many more people must start to reach your completes, which drives sample cost.
incidence.how: From a panel quote or a past wave: 40% means 100 starts for 40 completes.

rate_per_minute.title: Rate per minute
rate_per_minute.what: What your panel charges per minute of interview, per complete, at 100% incidence.
rate_per_minute.why: Cost per complete = rate × length ÷ incidence; it is the one number that turns length into money.
rate_per_minute.how: Take it from your supplier’s rate card. Nothing here guesses a price.

min_cpi.title: Minimum cost per complete
min_cpi.what: The floor your panel charges however short the survey is.
min_cpi.why: Short, high-incidence surveys would otherwise price below what any panel accepts.
min_cpi.how: Optional. Leave blank if your supplier has no minimum.

project_fee.title: Project fee
project_fee.what: Fixed costs on top of sample: programming, data processing, reporting.
project_fee.why: So the total is the number you actually quote.
project_fee.how: Optional; added once to the sample cost.

translationDraft.title: Model drafts
translationDraft.what: A model writes a first translation of every string that is still blank.
translationDraft.why: Translators check a draft faster than they write from nothing. Their own translations are never overwritten.
translationDraft.how: Type the language code and press Draft. Drafts that lose a piping token are refused. Download the sheet: drafted rows say "model draft — check". Only Bedrock or a local model is used — client text never goes to a free tier.

translations.title: Translations
translations.what: Field the same questionnaire in other languages from one master.
translations.why: Multi-country and multi-language studies stay one study: same codes, one data file, one set of tables.
translations.how: Type a language code (hi, ta, pt-BR), download the sheet, have it translated, upload it. Then add ?lang=hi to the survey link.

probes.title: Follow-up probes
probes.what: When an open answer is too short (“good”, “nothing”, under six words), the survey asks one more neutral question about it.
probes.why: Thin answers cannot be coded; one probe usually turns them into usable reasons, as a moderator would.
probes.how: Tick the “why” questions only — leave job titles or names unticked, where short is right. Links opened afterwards ask the probes.

crosscheck.title: Data vs questionnaire
crosscheck.what: Checks every answer in the data against what the questionnaire allows: codes, screen-outs, single answers, ranges.
crosscheck.why: A scripting error (a wrong code, a screen-out that did not fire) shows up here before it reaches the client.
crosscheck.how: Needs the questionnaire and the project data. Click “Check again”; open each discrepancy to see the respondents it affects.

findings.title: Key findings
findings.what: The main results, read off the tables: significant differences first, then the leading answers.
findings.why: Every number is cited to its table and base, so nothing in a headline can be invented.
findings.how: Read them here; the same findings open the PowerPoint. Grey chips show the table, column, % and base behind each number.

tracker.title: Waves and countries
tracker.what: Compares this study with other waves or countries of the same tracker, and stacks them into one file.
tracker.why: Before trending or pooling, you need to know what changed — a dropped question, a renumbered list, a code that now means something else.
tracker.how: Tick the other studies and Compare. Red items must be fixed before stacking; with one other wave picked, significant moves are listed.

methods.title: Advanced methods
methods.what: MaxDiff, TURF, Van Westendorp pricing and key-driver analysis on this study’s completes.
methods.why: The analyses usually done in a separate tool, computed from the same data as the tables.
methods.how: Pick a method (greyed ones need questions this study does not have), choose its inputs, and Run.

maxdiff.title: MaxDiff
maxdiff.what: Ranks items by importance from “most / least” choices: a score (times best − times worst, per time shown) and, when the file records which items each screen showed, a utility and share of preference.
maxdiff.why: Forced trade-offs separate items that all score “very important” on a rating scale.
maxdiff.how: Choose the exercise and Run. Scores run from −1 (always worst) to +1 (always best). Shares add to 100%: the chance each item is preferred over the others. One model for the whole sample, not per respondent.

turf.title: TURF
turf.what: Finds the set of options (flavours, channels, features) that reaches the most people — anyone choosing at least one.
turf.why: The most popular items often appeal to the same people; TURF picks the combination that adds new people.
turf.how: Choose a multi-select question and the largest set size, then Run. Reach is the share who chose at least one in the set.

van_westendorp.title: Van Westendorp pricing
van_westendorp.what: From four price questions (too cheap, a bargain, getting expensive, too expensive) finds the acceptable price range.
van_westendorp.why: Shows where price starts to hurt and where it raises doubts about quality, before a launch.
van_westendorp.how: Needs the four numeric price questions (the Pricing block in the builder adds them). Map each one, then Run.

drivers.title: Key drivers
drivers.what: Which attributes matter most for an overall rating: each attribute’s share of what explains it (Johnson’s relative weights).
drivers.why: Tells you what to improve first; unlike simple correlations it stays fair when attributes are related to each other.
drivers.how: Outcome: the overall rating (satisfaction, likelihood to recommend). Attributes: two or more rating questions on the same kind of scale — not gender or age. Then Run.

adverse_events.title: Adverse events in open answers
adverse_events.what: Reads every open answer for side effects, a medicine not working, overdose, pregnancy or misuse.
adverse_events.why: In health research, an event a respondent describes must be reported to the drug maker’s safety team within a working day.
adverse_events.how: Red items mean someone had it — read each and report the real ones. Mentions (nobody said they had it) are folded below.

cleaning.title: Cleaning review
cleaning.what: Respondents whose answers look unreliable, ranked by an authenticity score (0–100) with the reasons.
cleaning.why: Speeders, straight-liners, pasted or AI-written answers distort results; a person decides who is removed, with the evidence in front of them.
cleaning.how: Click a respondent to see their answers behind each flag. Keep (K) or Remove (R); the next one opens. Lock when none are left.

cleaning_checks.title: What the checks mean
cleaning_checks.what: Too fast: finished far quicker than most. Straight-lined: the same answer down a whole grid. Gibberish: keyboard mash. Pasted / few keystrokes: text not typed. AI-written: phrases a model leaves. Duplicate: the same answers as someone else.
cleaning_checks.why: Each is a known sign of a fake or careless respondent — but none is proof on its own.
cleaning_checks.how: Filter by a check to review all of one kind; read the evidence before deciding.

cleaning_authenticity.title: Authenticity score
cleaning_authenticity.what: 1.00 means nothing looked wrong; each warning sign (pasted answer, very fast, straight-lined grid, open end matching another respondent) lowers it.
cleaning_authenticity.why: One number to order your review, with the reasons beside it so you never trust it blindly.
cleaning_authenticity.how: Read the listed signals, then decide. The weights are a first setting and will be tuned on reviewed studies.

cleaning_habits.title: Suggested from your past decisions
cleaning_habits.what: A check you have removed almost every time (at least 9 in 10, over 10 or more decisions on 2 or more locked studies) shows up here when respondents in this study are flagged the same way.
cleaning_habits.why: So you do not repeat the same decision by hand on every study. It is only a prompt: nothing is removed until you press the button.
cleaning_habits.how: Review them to filter the list to that check, or Remove all to remove them together with a note saying why. Remove all can be undone by deciding each one again.

cleaning_lock.title: Lock cleaning
cleaning_lock.what: Freezes the decisions and makes a cleaned version of the data, which the tables and deliverables then use.
cleaning_lock.why: So everything delivered is built on one agreed set of respondents.
cleaning_lock.how: Available when no flagged respondent is left unreviewed. Only the owner can unlock, with a reason.

open_ends.title: Open ends
open_ends.what: The questions respondents answered in their own words, and their coding into categories (a codeframe).
open_ends.why: Coded answers can be counted and tabbed like any other question.
open_ends.how: “Code open questions” builds a codeframe from a sample and codes every answer. Answers the model is unsure of appear below for you to accept or correct.

control_room.title: Control room
control_room.what: Live fieldwork at a glance: completes against target, quota fill, interview length, incidence and each supplier.
control_room.why: Problems in field (a full quota, a supplier sending poor respondents) are cheapest to fix the day they start.
control_room.how: It updates by itself when a respondent finishes or is screened out, and at least every 30 seconds. “Updated” shows how fresh it is.

suppliers.title: Sample suppliers
suppliers.what: One row per live link: who supplies it, progress against target, quality, and what you owe them.
suppliers.why: Panels are paid per accepted complete; this shows which supplier sends good respondents and what to pay.
suppliers.how: Edit sets the supplier’s name, price and target. Reconciliation downloads the file the panel asks for at the end of field.

accepted.title: Accepted
accepted.why: Panels pay incentives and bill only for accepted completes.
accepted.how: Removing a respondent in Cleaning moves them from accepted to rejected here.

reconciliation.title: Reconciliation file
reconciliation.what: Every respondent id the panel sent, how their interview ended, and accepted or rejected (with the reason).
reconciliation.why: Panels need it to pay respondents and to bill you correctly.
reconciliation.how: Finish cleaning first, then download and send it to the supplier.

soft_launch.title: Soft launch
soft_launch.what: Holds the link after a first small batch of completes (e.g. 50).
soft_launch.why: Check the data for scripting errors before paying for the full sample.
soft_launch.how: Set the number here; when it is reached the link pauses. Check the batch, then release to full sample.

redirects.title: Vendor redirects
redirects.what: The panel addresses a respondent is sent to when they complete, are screened out, are over quota or fail security.
redirects.why: Panels count and pay respondents by where they land.
redirects.how: Paste the URLs your panel gives you; keep their {pid}/{rid} markers so each respondent’s id is passed back.

link_quotas.title: Quotas
link_quotas.what: Limits on how many completes each group can have (e.g. 200 women).
link_quotas.why: Keeps the sample representative; people in a full group are turned away as over quota.
link_quotas.how: Set them here, or once in the builder’s Quotas card so every new link starts with them.

test_link.title: Test link
test_link.what: A link for checking the survey yourself: jump to any question, fill it with made-up respondents.
test_link.why: Test answers never mix with real data.
test_link.how: Create it, try every route, then create the real link for fieldwork.

materialize.title: Build data file
materialize.what: Turns the link’s interviews into the project’s data file: one row per complete, a column per answer.
materialize.why: Tables, cleaning and reports read the data file, not the live interviews.
materialize.how: Click it whenever you want the latest completes in the tables (at soft launch and at the end of field).

dry_run.title: Dry run
dry_run.what: Sends made-up respondents through the questionnaire’s logic before any link exists.
dry_run.why: Shows who would be screened out, which questions nobody reaches, and dead ends — while it is still cheap to fix.
dry_run.how: Run it after approving the questionnaire; read each warning and fix the logic in the questionnaire.

logic_xray.title: Logic X-ray
logic_xray.what: Draws the questionnaire as a line of questions, with the paths simulated respondents took between them.
logic_xray.why: Shows at a glance where people skip, where they drop out, and which questions nobody reaches.
logic_xray.how: Select a question to see its share of respondents and where they go next.

fielded_data.title: Fielded data
fielded_data.what: The respondent data in this project as fieldwork: who is in it and how each interview ended.
fielded_data.why: A survey fielded on another platform is still this study’s fieldwork and can be checked the same way.
fielded_data.how: Upload or replace the file in the Data bar on the project page.

templates.title: Start from a template
templates.what: A complete questionnaire for a type of study, written the standard way, routing included.
templates.why: Faster and more consistent than writing every screener and scale from scratch.
templates.how: Pick one and fill in what it asks (category, brands…). Edit, add or delete questions afterwards.

blocks.title: Ready-made blocks
blocks.what: Standard sections — consent, screener, awareness, NPS, satisfaction, MaxDiff, pricing — with their wording, scales and logic.
blocks.why: Each comes with the details that are easy to get wrong: balanced scales, an exclusive “None of these”, randomised brand lists.
blocks.how: Select the question it should follow, open a block, fill its few fields and “Add block”.

expert_notes.title: Expert notes
expert_notes.what: The estimated interview length and notes a senior researcher would make: leading wording, two questions in one, missing “None”, lopsided scales, long grids.
expert_notes.why: These biases are cheap to fix now and impossible to fix after fieldwork.
expert_notes.how: Click the chip to read the notes; click a question id to jump to it. Notes are advice and never block saving.

quota_plan.title: Quota plan
quota_plan.what: The groups the sample must contain, as shares of the completes you need (e.g. Women 50% of 400).
quota_plan.why: Written once with the questionnaire, it is applied to every link opened afterwards.
quota_plan.how: Enter completes, add a row per group: a name, a question, then its answer(s) — or for a number question like age, a band (18 to 34) — and the share. Shares for one question must not exceed 100%.

ask_if.title: Ask this question only if
ask_if.what: A condition on earlier answers; people who do not meet it skip the question.
ask_if.why: So people are only asked what applies to them (e.g. satisfaction only from users).
ask_if.how: Pick the earlier question, how it compares, and the answer. Several conditions can all or any have to hold.

end_if.title: End the interview (screen out) if
end_if.what: A condition that ends the interview for people outside the target.
end_if.why: Screeners keep the sample to the people the study is about.
end_if.how: Usually on the question itself: “What is your age? is less than 18”.

thread.title: Study thread
thread.what: The trail behind one number in a table: its base, the question, cleaning, weighting and the data file.
thread.why: Anyone reading a figure can see exactly what it was computed from, so it can be checked instead of trusted.
thread.how: Click a number in a table. The trail opens on the right; press Escape to close it.

norms.title: Past-study norms
norms.what: The range this answer took in the agency's earlier studies that asked the same question with the same answer list.
norms.why: 34% means little alone; against a past range of 18–31% it is clearly high.
norms.how: Shown in the thread for the clicked row. It needs at least two matching past studies.

lifecycle.title: Lifecycle rail
lifecycle.what: Eight steps a study moves through, from the brief to the insight, each coloured by what is actually stored for this project.
lifecycle.why: You see at a glance what is done, what needs you and what has not started, without opening every tab.
lifecycle.how: Click a step to open it. A step marked "needs you" is also listed below the rail. Proof stays unstarted until dry-run results are kept.

report.title: Cited report
report.what: The report's sentences, each pointing at the table cells it rests on.
report.why: A sentence is the claim a client repeats. Code, not a model, checks every number, comparison and small base against the cited cells.
report.how: Draft report writes sentences from the findings. Click a sentence to edit it; a struck-through one failed the check and says what to change. Accepted sentences go on the deck's Report slide.

logic_certificate.title: Logic certificate
logic_certificate.what: A one-page PDF saying the approved questionnaire was checked by a senior researcher's rules and fielded against 1,000 made-up respondents.
logic_certificate.why: It is proof for the client that no question is unreachable and no rule is impossible before real people are paid for.
logic_certificate.how: Press Issue logic certificate. If it says Not issued, fix the questions it names and run it again.

field_close.title: Close fieldwork
field_close.what: Builds the data file, tables, report draft and decks from the completed interviews in one go.
field_close.why: One step instead of five, and every deliverable is built from the same data.
field_close.how: Press the button and confirm. It replaces earlier deliverables; interviewing is not stopped.
